Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. This motion is prompted today by the report of the Economic Council of Canada which pointed to what it called the "national disgrace" of unemployment caused by eight years of economic failure. Mr. Speaker, the report to which the hon. member refers is quite a comprehensive one and brings to light a number of factors that may have hitherto been unrecognized as sources of regional economic disparity. The hon. member will realize that the council places increasing emphasis on increasing productivity per worker in the areas of slow growth and addresses not only the federal government but also the provinces, underlining the necessity of a joint and new approach to the problem of economic disparity.
The hon. member will also realize that the comments of the council on the question of regionalized fiscal policy have already been met, or at least, recognized, by the actions taken in the budget by the Minister of Finance. There is no desire on the part of the government to conceal the seriousness of the problems that are disclosed in the Economic Council's report. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General.
Can the Solicitor General confirm or deny the information which I have received and which we have all read in the papers these past few days to the effect that on April 18 his department sent a telegram to the Leclerc Institute ordering the release of prisoner No. 8537, a Mr. Laurier Boutin?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LIBERATION OF MR. LAURIER BOUTIN BY TELEGRAM FROM LECLERC INSTITUTE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member's inquiry, I must say that Mr. Boutin had been first liberated under mandatory surveillance in October 1974 and that his imprisonment was to come to an end on October 12, 1975. At the time of his deportation from the United States to Canada in November 1976, a warrant had been issued to cancel his liberation order under mandatory surveillance. However, in the summer of 1976, the British Columbia courts found that the warrant to cancel his parole could not be executed because it had been issued after the expiry date of his parole. That is why, having reviewed the cases of 17 people detained under a warrant executed after the date of the parole or after the expiry date of the mandatory surveillance, the National Parole Board was under the legal obligation to release prisoner Boutin.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it would be my turn yesterday to speak on the budget, but still I thank the Chair for giving me the opportunity to do so today.
Mr. Speaker, as several previous speakers have shown we all agree that the Canadian economy is now reeling and that the federal government alone and not the provinces or the Pequiste government in Quebec is responsible. We now have the economic results of the government policies. As we all know, there are now in Canada more than one million registered unemployed people, quite apart from a million others who are not necessarily on the records of manpower and UIC centres.
Mr. Speaker, according to the present budget, the federal government is expecting another 200,000 unemployed people in 1977, which means that this government has led us to the worst employment crisis ever in Canadian history. Furthermore, the number of families living on welfare and not considered as part of the unemployed population has been increasing. Canada now has more than 750,000 families in this situation, which means that in 1977 2 million Canadians are living on welfare. It also means that 4 to 5 million people are depending on money doled out by the federal or provincial governments to the extent that these governments pay into welfare funds. And while we are complaining about unemployment and about the overly numerous people who must live on

The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
social welfare benefits, we see at the same time that Canadian man-hour productivity has been 50 per cent lower than in the U.S. with an average hourly wage which is twice what Americans get for the same job. As a result our prices are no longer competitive and we rely on imported products to meet our requirements. Mr. Speaker, we are now depending on other countries, even for essential goods. That is why the Canadian market is flooded with cheaper foreign products. In 1976, for example, 55 per cent of the shoes sold in Canada were imported. Yet the shoe industry was one of the oldest in the country.
This is the record of the former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin, who has been unable to solve the problem of the shoe industry in Canada as he was unable to solve the problem of the textile industry. And now he is paid $55,000 a year as chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board to solve the inflation problem which affects the entire Canadian economy. In 1976, furniture manufacturers followed on the heels of the shoe industry because 62 per cent of furniture sold in Canada during 1976 was imported. In the textile industry, the situation is even worse and we hear similar stories from other areas, namely agriculture and others.
From the point of view of economic conditions, businessmen, who are not imbeciles, will not risk borrowing money at 12 or 13 per cent interest on top of service charges. This would be a real interest rate of 18 per cent to invest in production. Mr. Speaker, the money business has grown more important than the production of life essentials.
In 1968 the interest rate was 6 per cent and one of the first moves of the present government, just after its accession to power, was to abolish the ceiling on interest rates to reward the world of finance. Now we have the following results: The interest rate has doubled since 1968 and while the worker works to become unemployed, interest rates have doubled and the world of finance is thriving and healthy.
Furthermore, while the different levels of government preach restriction to the Canadian people and invite them to tighten their belts, they empty their pockets with expenses of more than 55 per cent of the overall GNP while telling us about the unity of Canada to try to make us forget the economic disaster we are experiencing.
The federal government alone will spend more than $2,000 per capita in Canada in 1977, representing an average of over $10,000 per Canadian family. We will have to pay financiers some $5.35 billion in interests on federal bonds alone, that is to say $15 million a day in interest which we could easily avoid if we would call upon the financial services of the Bank of Canada, our own financial institution, on the basis of expenses incurred to finance our own federal bonds instead of relying on the private chartered banks which are electoral funds providers.
Mr. Speaker, once again in 1977 the budget provides for more than $1 billion under the foreign assistance program, not to mention long term loans bearing no interest which are

April 20, 1977
granted to various countries of the world. At the same time the federal government lends money to Canadian provinces at 10 or 12 per cent interest rates to have them participate in the so-called profitable federalism of the Prime Minister and of Canada.
National defence will cost more than $5 billion in 1977. Federal bureaucrats in all departments will cost over $8.5 billion, which means that more than $20 billion will be spent in Canada in 1977 to pay for our national defence, which at best exists only in theory, and to meet expenditures for public servants, interest charges on the public debt and foreign assistance. Mr. Speaker, if you add to that the cost of unemployment insurance and the cost of welfare incurred by the federal government, besides the amount paid by the provinces, we will spend in excess of $50 billion in 1977 to try to keep the artificial breath of our declining economy.
Before such an administration, Mr. Speaker, the worker who is lucky enough to keep on working with a good salary is penalized by taxes taken out of his wages, which makes him sick of working because he is deprived of the fruit of his labour while unemployment insurance and welfare or social assistance benefits reward fairly too well those who are the recipients, as compared to those working and bound to pay taxes.
In an economic climate as unhealthy socially as the present one, profits are no longer the normal incentive to business. Rip-offs have become quite common in business. When we see, for instance, that goods bought for $6 sell for $25, this is not normal and business has truly become a regular rip-off. The system is so unsound that one cannot expect to live on profits, since it is too expensive. People want to become rich immediately since they do not know what can happen tomorrow morning.
The social and economic climate of insecurity in business causes everyone to seek not profits, but business lottery, like Foto-Canada ticket. The economic climate is the result of past administrations who governed for the benefit of finance, which is growing wealthier every day at the expense of the workers who get poorer day by day. Instead of coming to grips with the root causes of the evil, this Liberal government in its last budget deals with the symptoms of our sick economic system, like a carpenter acting on the advice of so-called experts would repair the roof of a house when he should be fixing the crumbling foundations. In order to truly remedy what is wrong in our economy, Mr. Speaker, the last budget should have contained measures designed to lower the interest rates to 6 per cent, or to the same level as before 1968 and before inflation.
Second, the government should cut defence expenditures by 50 per cent. Third, it should provide a guaranteed annual income to everyone through the Bank of Canada so as to cut unemployment insurance and welfare costs and enable those now on welfare and unemployment insurance to work if they are able to do so and to supplement the guaranteed annual income they would receive. Thus, thousands of people now on welfare and thousands of unemployed could work and improve their standards of living while performing some tasks that are
April 20,1977

essential to the Canadian economy. For instance, producers could hire them to pick potatoes in the fall instead of letting them rot or of bringing in Haitians like they did in my area and have been doing nearly every year.
For example, they could pick potatoes or work on some essential public or community projects. Unemployed and welfare recipients could lead a more dignified life instead of always having to depend on others. The guaranteed annual revenue financed by the Bank of Canada would allow the various governments to cut at least by half the extremely high administration costs of unemployment insurance and social welfare. Let us not forget that the federal bureaucracy, with all its departments cost more than $8,600 million in 1976, and in 1977 will cost almost $9 billion. This money saved on bureaucracy could be reinvested in order to help small businesses in competition with foreign and domestic firms as well as with large businesses which smother the smaller ones that now receive more government subsidies.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, we should use the Bank of Canada to lend at a rate which would just cover the administration costs, or 1 per cent, the amounts required by municipalities, cities, school boards and provincial governments, so that instead of having to go to New York, Boston or elsewhere, those various administrations may obtain funds at the rate of 1 per cent in order to carry out major and essential public investment projects. Then, they could cut taxes for the benefit of small homeowners, since they would have lower interests to pay to international finance. This measure alone, Mr. Speaker, would make it possible to effect positive changes in the Canadian economy.
I also wish to emphasize that in the last three years, our balance of payments deficit has increased by more than $11 billion. Our total deficit now exceeds $40 billion, which means that we bought from other countries $40 billion worth of goods more than we sold to them, and what is worse, Mr. Speaker, the goods we export are mostly unprocessed raw materials, non-renewable resources, and soon Canada will have to import products manufactured from these materials. We have a trade deficit of more than $40 billion and soon Canada will have to pay or devaluate its currency. Once more, Canadian consumers will be penalized, since they will have to pay a debt incurred with a devaluated currency. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, West Germany, the country of the bad Germans of 1939 against whom we fought and won, have a trade surplus of $37 billion, exactly the opposite of Canada which won the war. All countries who won the war against Germany owe it now more than $37 billion. Germany lost the war in Europe that lasted six years, but won the economic war in the last 30 years. Germany is showing surpluses, while we have a trade deficit of over $40 billion.
Mr. Speaker, Canada now owes its shirt to other countries. Germany has accumulated a $37 billion surplus against those countries which cannot help getting into debt. Mr. Speaker, 1 really wonder who has won or lost the war.
1 should like to point out to my colleagues that in 1975, Canadian taxpayers paid $12,709 million in income tax, and
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
companies, $5,748 million. In 1976, taxpayers paid $14,889 million and companies, $5,210 million. In 1977 taxpayers will pay $15,620 million and companies $5,760 million. In other words, the taxpayers will have to pay more and more income tax while companies will get a break. Of course, Mr. Speaker, companies know better how election funds operate.
In the March 1976 issue of Quest magazine, one could read this:
In every five-day week we work two days for the government. We pay taxes we never heard of. We pay taxes on taxes and we spend more on taxes than anything else. Taxes shot up a staggering 239 per cent in the years between 1961 and 1975, family income went up 142 per cent, the cost of shelter 128 per cent and food 66 per cent.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the matter of Canadian energy, a most important issue. Oil companies keep on hiking their prices with the benevolent approval of governments; I will give statistics since these price hikes amount to a new form of hidden tax which the governments can blame on world wide oil price increases. They have even invented an artificial energy crisis in order to camouflage their hypocritical tax. From 1965 to 1969, the price of a barrel of oil at the well-head was $2.98. Profit on that barrel was $1.27. The federal tax amounted to 14 cents. Provincial taxes or royalties were 30 cents. Production costs for a barrel were 87 cents.
Because of successive price hikes up to January 1st 1977, the price of a barrel of oil at that date was $9.75 at the wellhead, that is a corporate profit of $3.63, $1.54 for federal taxes, $3.90 for provincial taxes or royalties and a production cost of 68 cents per barrel instead of 87 cents in 1965. While the production cost decreased by 19 cents, the sales price jumped from $2.58 to $9.78 a barrel, an accrual of $7.17 a barrel for an increase in corporate profits of $2.36 per barrel, $1.40 in federal taxes and $3.60 for various provincial taxes.
Mr. Speaker, all those who are blaming it on an energy crisis are getting their piece of the cake paid for by Canadian citizens. This faked energy crisis has once more enabled the government to hoodwink Canadian taxpayers with misleading advertising from these companies and to picks taxpayers' pockets each time they fill up their gastanks or turn up their thermostats in their homes.
The oil crisis, concocted by multinationals in conjunction with governments, is nothing but another hypocritical tax which enables governments to earn revenues to finance their extravagances and pay $20 million daily in interests, including $15 million on the national debt and $5 million on debts incurred by Crown corporations. Since I rose for my 20 minute speech, the national debt has increased by $274,000 and we have to pay $300,000 in interests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be well within that period. I wish we had television in this House. I have wished it many, many times. There is no other way in which we can convey to the people of Canada what is going on in this place.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) introduced his budget on Thursday night, March 31. The following day, the proceedings of the legislature in Toronto were televised and I went home that night to watch extracts on the television screen. I saw the government spokesman, the Hon. Darcy McKeough, say that it was a good federal budget. I saw the leader of the opposition, Mr. Stephen Lewis, attack it in the most strident terms. These are two parties represented in the opposition in this House, Mr. Speaker, and it seems to me there was a bit of truth-one could say a moment of truth- when these two parties, not friends of the Liberal government, discussed the budget in the capital of the province of Ontario, Toronto, some 250 miles from here.
Mr. McKeough knew that the federal Minister of Finance had very few options before him. We have a serious threat of inflation which must be restrained. We have levels of unemployment that are much higher than we want them to be, and something has to be done to create jobs. We have a crisis in our balance of payments, and we have a falling currency. Within this situation, there is very limited room to manoeuvre. On the other hand, Mr. Lewis, the leader of the opposition,
(Mr. Kaplan.)
who is perhaps the best representative of what has been known as "the British disease" to strike our television scene in many a day, said the government had to spend a lot more money to create direct jobs, those temporary jobs which would vanish when the government's spending ended. He wanted to spend. At the same time, he would have been the first to criticize the government if the fires of inflation had been fuelled through his advice being accepted.
I think it is no accident that the two provincial budgets which have been brought down very recently-in the province of Quebec by the Parti Quebecois finance minister, Mr. Pari-zeau, and in Toronto by the provincial treasurer, Darcy McKeough-are in very much the same mould as the federal budget which we are discussing. Others preceding me have outlined the specific details. There is some direct job creation-$100 million more, for a total of $458 million-but, as the minister pointed out, these are not career jobs, not the long-term employment that our young people are seeking. They are jobs which will end when government spending for this purpose ends.
There are tax reductions. All of these matters have been outlined. The tax reductions are to encourage small business, to give the average taxpayer something. But the scope for tax reductions is limited-a total of $1.17 billion. The program of restraint in government expenditures will continue. As the hon. member for Ottawa West, I am pleased to rise and support the budget, although the constituency I represent will be one of those feeling the impact of restraint in government expenditures, especially in the public service field, as much as any constituency in Canada.
The budget projects financial requirements in the order of $6.4 billion, but the minister was quick to say that he did not wish to pre-empt the private sector. He wants to put as little pressure as possible on the funds available for private investment. But this is still an expansionary budget. Cash requirements of this order are going to present a challenge to the monetary and financial institutions of this country.
The anti-inflation program is to be continued because we are not out of the woods yet. The minister indicated that a phasing-out program could not begin before October. He has expressed, however, in this place, the hope that the program itself can be terminated within the original time frame; that is, three years.
The major thrust of the budget, Mr. Speaker, is to encourage the private sector to create jobs. This is going to be denounced by some members on the other side of the House as inadequate, but if we stop to think about it, the jobs that are to be created in private industry are the kind of jobs with career expectations, the kind of jobs that give more satisfaction, the kind of jobs that represent a more permanent contribution to the Canadian economy. We are all painfully aware that wages in Canada are something like 10 per cent higher than in the United States, although this is not easy to measure. Indeed, in
April 20,1977

this period of changing exchange rates the comparison is even more difficult to make.
We are very much aware that productivity in Canada is very much lower than that in the United States, our major trading partner, and we also know that the measurement of productivity is subject to very serious limitations. If specific studies are made in areas such as the electrical equipment industry, for example, it is very possible to demonstrate the serious gap which exists between Canadian productivity and productivity in the country of our major trading partner.
I welcome the budget as representing the only thing that is possible in the circumstances we face. There was a time in which finance ministers were presented in the aspect of Santa Claus with goodies to be given to everybody. Unfortunately, there can be no Santa Claus at this time. The notion that the budget can be criticized because there is nothing in it for one group in society or for another falls far short of recognizing the true purpose of the budget, which is to encourage moderate expansion of the economy and create jobs where they are absolutely essential in the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, I have some criticisms to make of the budget. Frankly, I think more should have been done in the field of energy policy. I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is in the House and I look forward to hearing from him in connection with the further development of policy in the field of energy. I am not ashamed of our record, but I think we can do more and better than has been done so far. I would like to have seen measures to remove taxes from insulating materials. I note that the province of Ontario did take measures of this kind in the budget delivered last night. I would like to have seen a lead in the field of urban transit. One of the great disappointments to me is the silence of the budget on this issue.
The party to which I belong made a specific promise in the course of the 1974 election, one of which we are very much aware. In the field of energy conservation it would be possible for Canada to take action by bringing forward a long-term policy for urban and interurban transport. We might, for example, have undertaken measures to develop a technology suited to our northern climate. We have serious problems in moving people to and from their places of employment during our harsh winters. The basic technology has been inadequately developed. This is an area into which we could put federal funds with the very minimum of constitutional challenge, and I believe it is unfortunate that the budget did not take initial steps to develop a public transit policy as a means of saving petroleum resources which are so badly needed.
There is another area about which I, personally, feel very strongly. I realize that my hon. friends are not going to agree with me on this. I find it difficult to reconcile the fact that though nothing is provided for urban transit, $200 million more is set aside for the milk subsidy. It is true that $150 million of that sum is not a cash requirement of the budget but a write-off of expenses incurred in marketing surplus milk powder and a few other things. I am told that $48 million is in addition to the current subsidy. For the life of me I cannot
The Budget-Mr. Hees
make sense out of the marketing boards and what they are doing in the way of rationalizing the industry, providing a suitable product for the consumer, or even regulating the supply which is brought onto the market. By the standards according to which I have tried to judge the policy, I find it incomprehensible.
I intend to vote for the budget. I intend to support it because I think it is the right budget for Canada at this time. The phase through which the world economy is passing is a very difficult one to interpret, not only for ourselves but for the countries with which we are most closely associated-the economies of the western European powers, North America, Japan, Australasia. The prosperity for which we are looking has been very slow in emerging from our neighbour to the south as a result of current economic difficulties. There is no doubt in my mind that later this year the Minister of Finance will have to look at matters again, and it is only right that he should do so, along with Darcy McKeough in Ontario and Jacques Parizeau in Quebec and others who have considered in a responsible way what we can do at this time by way of budgetary policy. I am going to cast my vote in favour of the budget, and at the appropriate time I hope to register my concern as to the lack of an urban transit policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with a million unemployed people in this country and the prospect of an increase in that number as the year goes on, it is obvious that we must look for new and practical ways to find permanent jobs for a very large number of our fellow Canadians. I believe that one of the more important ways we can do this is to process more of our raw materials to their finished state.
For far too long we have been shipping out of this country a far too large proportion of our primary products to be processed to their final stages of production in other countries which thereby gain the many advantages of employment, taxes and profits which accrue from this further processing. We have in Canada the skilled manpower, managerial skill, cheap power and excellent transportation facilities which are needed for this further processing and it is about time we started doing something about getting more of this work for Canada.
Now, what should and can be done? Thirty years ago the government of Ontario introduced a plan which has been largely responsible for the spectacular expansion of the pulp and paper industry in that province during the intervening years. It required companies to process in the province a far higher proportion of the logs which they cut, a large proportion of which they had been shipping in the raw state to paper mills in the United States. What has worked so well in the case of the pulp and paper industry in Ontario can work equally well in other primary industries right across the country. It should apply to all raw materials which we ship to other countries for further processing, and can succeed equally well because of the great dependence of other countries on our primary products to feed their manufacturing processes.

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Martin
It is obvious that a certain proportion of the raw materials we produce must be exported in the raw state, but not nearly the proportion that is the case today. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should now undertake an intensive study of our primary industries to determine what proportion of the primary products we produce can reasonably be required to be processed to their finished state in this country.
Having decided what proportions of our various primary products should be further processed in Canada, we must produce an incentive which will be sufficiently attractive to persuade those who normally export our raw materials that it will be profitable for them to build the plants which will be necessary to carry out this additional processing in Canada. It has become painfully obvious that the grants now provided by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, although useful, have not proved sufficiently attractive to bring to our areas of slow growth sufficient new industry to reverse the dangerously high rates of unemployment that have persisted in those areas for many years.
I believe that in addition to the DREE grants which are now available to areas of slow growth, we must also make available an additional incentive in the form of a graduated scale of federal taxation which will permit new plants processing primary products in areas of slow growth to pay no federal taxes in the first full year of profitable operation, and gradually increase its tax payments until it is paying full taxation in the fifteenth year. My conversations with leading businessmen across the country have convinced me that this incentive, added to the present DREE grants for slow growth areas, will prove sufficiently attractive to accomplish what has to be done.
In the following ways these incentives will pay for themselves many times over in the years ahead. First, we can drastically cut the present far too high expenditure on unemployment insurance by stimulating the economy and enabling people to find work. Second, we can greatly increase tax revenues, because more people will be working and paying income taxes, more commodities will be sold and the buyers paying additional commodity taxes, and the increased volume of business will lower the unit cost of production and make available more profits to tax. I strongly urge the government to adopt this suggestion for providing employment for a large number of our people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the budget debate. Also, I want to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) and members on the other side who agreed to a time limitation of 20 minutes on the debate. I hope this is the kind of reform that most members of this House would be delighted to see become a permanent feature. I think that what cannot be said in 20 minutes in the House by any of us is probably not worth saying anyway.
I want to commence my comments this afternoon by making some very praiseworthy comments, which I think are quite justified, about the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for the kind of budget he has produced and the vision he has
[Mr. Hera.)
shown in a difficult time in our economy. I do not think that my words are taken out of context with the kind of support that has been shown by many outstanding leaders in this country. Although I would not normally look in this direction for support for a budget brought down by the government in Ottawa, 1 think it is noteworthy to quote an excerpt from the budget speech delivered yesterday by the provincial treasurer of Ontario, which in many ways was along the lines of the budget delivered here in Ottawa. He said that without profits there is no investment, that without investment there are no new jobs, no productive and non-inflationary jobs.
I think that is a fact of life. I think it is a fact which the government has very clearly recognized right through the piece. At this time perhaps more than any other it has come forward in sharp focus in the budget presentation of March 31. At some point in time we shall have to find the means of explaining to people generally that profits in themselves are not evil. It is what is done with profits that is so important. Basically, profits are an essential part of the engine of industry, and the minister recognizes this. I think all members on this side of the House recognize it, and I think most people who are anxious to secure meaningful employment, jobs which are long-lasting and are not temporary work measures, realize it as well.
I think that that comment of the provincial treasurer yesterday is a very important one which Canadian society must understand more and more. I also think business has the responsibility to tell its side of the story much more effectively than it has in the past. It has a great social responsibility to ensure that the kinds of benefits which will flow from this kind of budget will indeed be passed on in the form of additional jobs during a time of serious unemployment and when increasing unemployment appears to be on the horizon.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, the budget recognizes that at a time of higher than usual unemployment levels there is also a need for government to look at the situation and to ask itself: Can industry alone handle the problem, or does there need to be a little bit of pump-priming, as it were, from federal sources? The response that the government has come forward with is a Canada Works program and a Young Canada Works program which will have the effect of creating 600,000 man-months of work in this country over the next while. The amount of money involved is $458 million.
Although a number of people criticize these kinds of projects, when one looks at the fantastic employment figure involved 1 think such criticism has to be tempered with a measure of understanding that indeed this kind of added incentive to the economy is probably essential with unemployment levels as high as they are.
I have indicated that we are facing difficult circumstances under which the minister has to work. These are difficult economic times not only for Canadians but for the world. It is ridiculous for any member of this House to suggest that we can resolve problems in our economy without paying any
April 20, 1977

attention to what happens elsewhere. Canadians do not live in a vacuum, no more than people in any other country.
The United States of America is our best customer; we are their largest supplier. When their economy slows down, it is obvious that some plants in Canada will slow down. A plant in my riding that produces General Motors' vans will not make vans if people in the United States are not buying them. There are only two such plants in North America. They are not going to make them in Scarborough; it is as simple as that. It is terribly important, whether we like it or not, to realize the facts of life that we have to the south of us. They have an economy that is ten times the size of ours. If it improves, it will redound to our benefit. Of course, when it slows down we will feel it. On that score it is worth noting that the recent improvements taking place in the American economy have been noted recently in a number of financial publications. The demand for automobiles, the demand for houses and other major goods in that country is moving up on a very substantial curve. This is excellent medicine for our own idle plant capacity.
The leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) indicated that we are operating our plants in Canada at approximately 80 per cent capacity. Obviously, it would be better to move that figure up to 85 per cent or 90 per cent. The way that can be done is for more of our goods to be bought. The way that will happen is for the economy of the United States, as well as Canada and other countries to which we export, to improve so that they can absorb more of our goods. This is why the news on the horizon in the United States is extremely encouraging.
If the Canadian executives of industrial plants in this country can be convinced that what is happening in the United States is real and is not just illusory, then the budget measures which the Minister of Finance has introduced should work themselves into our system. They should be able to make maximum use of them and show it in terms of added employment as the year progresses and on into 1978.
The economy of the United States is moving ahead at the kind of pace I have demonstrated, and the figures are showing. The economy of the United States is coming back on the rails. This is extremely important, as I have indicated. It will have a direct impact on what goes on in this country. It is something of which we have to be very conscious. In the automotive business we have 7 per cent, and capital investment is expected to rise this year and next year in the United States. This will provide a tremendous potential stimulus for what will develop over the next two years.
Some evidence of the reality of the improvement in the United States economy is the fact that their Congress has been somewhat reluctant to pass the proposal put forward by President Carter for the $50 tax rebate to individual Americans. The reason they are reluctant to pass such a proposal at the present time is that the measure may no longer be needed. It was to act as a stimulus to the economy. Members of Congress, who are, after all, representatives of the public at large, are getting the feedback and the feeling that this kind of
The Budget-Mr. Martin
stimulus may no longer be needed. They are concerned, as we are concerned, that there should not be an artificial stimulus put into the economy if it will have a serious adverse effect on inflationary problems.
The aggravation of inflationary pressures is very much with us and is very much a problem with which we must continue to cope. The suggestion is that if the stimulus is put into effect in the United States, in spite of some objection in Congress, the gross national product in that country might go up some 6 per cent by the end of the year. They are anticipating an improvement in the productivity rate of some V/i per cent, which is in the form of an added kicker to the rather good picture that is showing down there.
I have taken some time to point out this very important development, because it is very much like being a manufacturer selling to one of the large department stores. If the department store has a drop-off in its business, then the manufacturer, obviously, will have a drop-off in what goes on in his plant, resulting in the lay-off of employees. If the department store starts to pick up-as I suggested the United States economy is doing-and it is a big customer, then things will go much better in your plant. That is the kind of scene we are looking at in Canada. That is the kind of scene that the Minister of Finance had the foresight to look at and take into account in preparing his budget.
The budget is a cautious document at a time when we need caution. We cannot afford to throw away the gains we have made through controls. We must be careful of that. We must reinforce, in Canadians, the will power to fight inflation. We must adopt an attitude of keeping down inflation. It is still the number one problem. We must not expect our economy to skyrocket. We must be prepared for higher energy and food costs. These are problems that we would certainly not wish upon ourselves, but which will, indeed, be present, and there is very little we can do about them.
Given these things, the outlook is promising. The rate of inflation has been lowered by controls. Government expenditures are down by $750 million from the amount forecast in the budget last year. The target for 1977-78 is $650 million less than the expenditure plan announced in February by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). The growth plan for 1977-78 is only an increase of 9.8 per cent over last year. That is lower than the expected increase in the gross national product. It is also lower than the 11 per cent increase predicted in the last budget. This budget will help speed the pace of economic recovery. In 1977 we can look forward to the gross national product being 4 per cent higher in volume and as much as 11 per cent higher in value than that of 1976.
In the time remaining I would like briefly to review some of my concerns. In our democratic system, within our party members are able to put forward concerns for the various procedures which we have to ensure that government policies reflect or give an opportunity for all members to make their contributions and voice their concerns. One of the concerns is in the area of energy conservation. As chairman of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, I

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Martin
feel we need more government direction in this area. We need to concentrate on long-term strategies. That is evident.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) was in the House this afternoon and made the point that it is far cheaper to conserve a barrel of oil than to discover, develop and bring to market new barrels of oil. He also made the point that we must spend money on conservation measures. The budget has indicated that we will continue developing our energy supplies as well as developing better conservation practices. My only concern is that the focus may not be as sharp and as serious as we will need. I look forward to increasing measures in this direction as the years progress.
In the area of unemployment, I was concerned, as I am sure other members were, about the increasing rate. There was a feeling among many of us that gentle stimulation was needed in that area. That gentle stimulation has been provided, with care, to ensure that the kind of stimulation put into the picture will not unduly increase our rate of inflation. I mentioned the job creation program that was increased by $100 million to a total of $458 million.
In the area of capital investment, I am most conscious of the Economic Council of Canada estimates that we will need $850 billion in this country over the next ten years. 1 am very pleased that the budget is doing a number of things to encourage investment by ordinary Canadians in the private sector, so that as much as possible of our new investment in this country can be provided by Canadians and, therefore, we will not have to resort more than absolutely necessary to going outside our country to seek the capital that we need.
I was also encouraged, in the area of investment, by the kind of incentives for small businesses and venture enterprises that are provided in the budget, because they are the backbone of our economy. Independent businessmen generally have voiced their approval of this budget, of what the government is doing and of the fact that this budget will give them an opportunity to create more jobs by expanding their facilities and to go on with the work of producing the kinds of goods they are able to produce.
I cannot complete my remarks without indicating one area of disappointment which, as a member of a large urban community-namely, metropolitan Toronto-has concerned me for some time; that is, the need for assistance in the area of urban transit. Again I say that I am not entirely clear whether this is an area in which the federal government should be directly involved over the long term. Nevertheless, I feel that we did make a commitment some years ago, and although that commitment has been met to the extent of approximately one-third, we must consider spending the remaining $200 million on measures that will give metropolitan Toronto and other major urban areas the kind of stimulus they need to get on with important matters relating to urban transit which are direct offshoots of our conservation programs, such as encouraging people to leave their private automobiles at home

when they go to work. This is an involved subject, but I believe that we must continue to look at it.
With regard to the transportation strategy which we must develop, I have mentioned in past debates in the House that I believe we need a better mingling of our transportation systems by air, train and bus, so that perhaps for trips of over 500 miles we should concentrate on the use of aeroplanes, for trips of between 200 miles and 500 miles we should concentrate on rail service, and for trips of under 200 miles we should consider travelling by bus. This is a time when Canadians must move around this country. We must do all we can to encourage people from Quebec, from the west and from other regions to intermingle and to discuss their concerns and listen to the concerns of others. It is an important area, in my view, in terms of the national unity that we are trying to develop in our country at this time.
One other area on which I would urge the government to concentrate in its forthcoming social legislation is help for the disabled. They are not numerous in terms of percentages. When a breadwinner suddenly finds himself disabled, from whatever cause, he is in a terrible plight today if he has a family to look after. Much has been done for the elderly, although more needs to be done, there is considerable concentration on the problems of young people, but the disabled group, which falls in the middle, people who suddenly find themselves incapacitated and can no longer earn their livelihood, should receive greater assistance. This is an area to which I believe the government should address itself in the future. I realize the problems at present in bringing in programs involving additional expenditures, but I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and others on the government benches seriously to consider-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the attitude should be of a member taking part in the debate on the budget presented on March 31 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I do not know if it should be the approach of a beggar approaching a bank manager, or of a millionnaire temporarily reduced to selling apples on the street corner approaching his client. Perhaps by the time I have completed my speech I will not be any wiser as to which of the courses I will adopt.
However, I would like to make six points. The first is with regard to the deficit. Our deficit financing is in the order of $6 billion or $7 billion this year. It was $1 billion less in the last fiscal year. These are deficits that occurred in good times. I pose this philosophical or financial question: What would have happened had those deficits been run up in bad times, and how
April 20, 1977

would we have handled them? Are there any studies under way, any papers produced by learned scholars, or unlearned ones, as to the effect that this deficit financing will have on us in future years? 1 know not and, as anybody who knows me obviously appreciates, I am not in the fiscal stream. It concerns me. If we cannot manage our affairs better when we have supposedly good times, why should we expect our affairs to be more manageable in the future when the deficit we are running up now is thrust upon other shoulders?
The Globe and Mail put it rather well in its editorial on March 31, the morning of the presentation of the budget by the Minister of Finance. The article reads in part as follows:
The government has achieved a budgetary surplus only once in the past ten years. Federal debt obligations have nearly doubled, to $42.2 billion, between 1966 and 1976. Servicing that debt had climbed from $1.2 billion to $4.7 billion.
That is almost a fourfold increase over ten years. Does it, or does it not, give us pause in this place? Apparently it does not. But it is still a question we must ask. In the article, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is quoted as saying:
"As a country", Mr. Clark said, "we have become the world's largest borrower of international capital... These figures reflect a country which lives not only on borrowed dollars but on borrowed time, a country which has lost its competitive edge in the world".
When I look around, I realize that all 264 of us in the House of Commons are presented every day of the week with bills and I wonder how we would run our personal affairs, pay our bills and run our households if we adopted the attitude we have toward national financing. There may be a philosophy which says that each and every one of us is here to make a determination that the country known as Canada should carry on its back a debt load which will be passed on from generation to generation to the end of time. I suppose that would be fair enough if you considered that debt load as you would a mortgage which can be a perpetual mortgage because the country will always remain the type of country that is able to handle it.
It is not as if you and I were dealing with a debt load on our homes, knowing that we are getting older and might not be able to handle it. The fact is that in this country a certain number of people enter the work force at the age of 16 and continue to work for many productive years. So perhaps the answer that we must acknowledge is, that there has to be some kind of mortgage hanging over our lives so long as we continue as citizens and can handle it. But I wish somebody would spell it out for me instead of bringing out the figures which I have been seeing in my more than 15 years in parliament.
Secondly, I intend to say something nice about the budget. It will be a quick reference, so I hope hon. members opposite will listen to what I have to say before I go on to something else. I think that the concession regarding deductions for income tax purposes, the capitalization under the DREE program, is probably a fair one. It gives an opportunity for companies in Atlantic Canada, for example, where the problem is greatest, to use the income tax system and DREE to their best advantage. It is one of those technical things that
The Budget-Mr. McCIeave
has not been spelled out. We have not been presented with any paper which says it is a good thing, or what it is expected to achieve; but I think it probably recognizes something which I have always thought should be recognized, and that is that if we are going to have a Department of Regional Economic Expansion, we should recognize the philosophy that there are parts of the country needing more help than other parts.
In this regard I say to my friends opposite-I think they would probably concede this-that the five eastern provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are the provinces which have not progressed as well as they should in recent times. I think the Minister of Finance should be complimented for that particular step in his budget, and I hope it has the effect for which the minister hopes.
1 would like to turn to the third point in my remarks. I raised this matter with the Minister of Finance the other day. During the recess I met a young man who is in the construction industry-which is having its own difficulties, as one can appreciate-and who had a common law liaison with a woman. There are two children as a result of that liaison. He has since moved to a different relationship with another woman, but he is still obligated to look after the children of his previous liaison.
When I raised this matter the other day with the minister, I think he stated the law quite properly when he said that the Department of National Revenue does not give common law partners the same rights under the law as it gives somebody who is a member of a regular marriage. In this case, this man terminated his prior relationship but is responsible for looking after the children. He has been called upon to pay $700 or $800, and in no way has he a chance to claim anything when he files his income tax return before the end of this month.
I think that is wrong, and I think the Minister of Finance recognized, when he replied to me yesterday, that it was probably wrong. At least his department and the Department of National Revenue have initiated studies with regard to this question. I raise this matter on behalf of a very ordinary taxpayer in my constituency. If we cannot change the law or the practice, the effect on that young man will be grievous. He will have no incentive to go anywhere or to do anything about meeting his obligations either to the woman to whom he was once married in a commonlaw sense or to the woman to whom he is now married in a very proper sense, or to the children of both liaisons.
This is not a partisan issue, but surely it is an issue which must be of concern to anybody around here who seeks justice. It is something we have to deal with, and I hope soon. Money has been paid, and is being paid, under a proper court order. The court has recognized that the man has an obligation to the two children of the common law relationship. Surely it could be part of our housekeeping changes in the law, which started last year, to deal with this matter. I am probably arguing on behalf of thousands of people across Canada, but I am talking about one particular case in my constituency. I hope the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. McCleave
(Miss Begin) will turn their departments toward coming up with a very quick answer in this regard.
I should like to turn to the question of capital gains. Hon. members will realize that my approach is not consecutive. I was a member of the committee which considered the Benson white paper. I was involved with the whole thing until it finally came to pass a number of years back. I wonder if the capital gains tax is really achieving the purpose we thought it would achieve. I understand that the tax from both the federal and provincial points of view achieved about $54 million in 1972, about $84 million in 1973, about $90 million in 1974, and perhaps $100 million in 1975. These estimates were provided in the Globe and Mail of October 14, 1976.
If these figures are correct-and I imagine they are; certainly, the first figures are correct-the capital gains tax revenue would not even cover government expenses for one day, and they provide about one-third of 1 per cent of the total revenue of government. Under those circumstances, and knowing the crying need of the country to have capital invested, I wonder whether that sort of tax is really worth it, or whether one should take the very serious view that because the realization is so small with regard to the over-all revenue that is raised perhaps it should be abolished. I do not know, but I raise this as a very serious philosophical question, because obviously we are in a period when capital investment is almost at stagnation and this question is of concern to most members of parliament.
To carry the theme a little further, we are also under a fair amount of pressure from the farming community to re-think the capital gains tax as it applies to farms which are not owned by individuals, but by a corporation or some form of partnership. I think we should re-examine what the capital gains tax is doing not just to farmers but to all Canadians. For example, the very legitimate argument is made to myself and others that a farm which is close to a city in Ontario is very different from a grain farm in the western provinces which may be between two cities but very remote from both of them, so that one person's possible gold mine is just a living to another person. I think that should be part of the study which I suggest should be carried out.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the other burning question-the first being the economy of the country, the other being the state of the nation, or national unity. I hope to deal with it in a reasonably positive fashion. A couple of days ago the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) put a question to the government House leader about getting parliament involved. Something that bothers Canadians is that from what they regard as the heart of Canada, this parliament, not enough has been^aid. I think this is a very justifiable criticism, Mr. Speaker. The other place moved very quickly on the matter. Even if one can criticize the other place, one can never say it did not respond rather quickly to the national unity issue.
For what it is worth, 1 suggest that the House leaders should set aside a certain period over the next year for members who

wish to make submissions on what should be done about national unity and the questions that will confront us when Premier Levesque presents his referendum. This could be 30 minutes every evening from six o'clock, Monday to Thursday. It would give each member an opportunity to speak on a very, very important topic. I do not think it should necessarily be tied to any particular motion unless a very general one such as: We all believe in Canada. That almost sounds like motherhood.
Half an hour every evening would allow members to contribute to the continuing debate and comment on things like the figures issued by the Quebec government or those issued yesterday by the Ontario government which also set off a hot debate. I suppose other governments, and even this House, will be able to set up their own figures. At least over the next critical year members would have an opportunity to be heard on this important matter and add to a debate that is very necessary for the future of Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the debate on the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). This is a budget designed to meet many of the serious problems Canada faces today and which every western industrialized country faces; that is, the problems of inflation, unemployment, our competitive position in the world, the energy crisis and the economic turmoil which resulted from it.
The budget seeks to reduce inflation by maintaining the Anti-Inflation Board's program until the fall. This will give business, industry and government an opportunity to negotiate a way to maintain the restraints on wages and prices for some time ahead. The government has indicated that it plans to reduce its expenditures by some $640 million below its estimates tabled a few months ago. A good deal of stimulus has been provided to the Canadian economy by a reduction in taxes of more than $1 billion with the indexing of old age security payments, guaranteed income supplements and family allowances in January of this year. The budget provides for a further $1 billion reduction in taxes to industry and individuals through incentives to industry by means of the investment tax credit, the inventory allowance of 3 per cent and various investment incentives.
More important to low-income families is the increase in the employment expense allowance from $150 to $250 and the credit against federal income tax of $50 per child. These combined measures will reduce taxes for families with four children, with an income of $10,000 upwards, by at least $200 a year, which will be a welcome relief.
Another problem that we face during this period is a rapidly expanding labour force. From 1965 to 1980 our labour force will grow by 50 per cent, whereas in most European countries the increase will be from 5 per cent to 15 per cent and in the United States it will be about 30 per cent. On top of the other problems we face, we have the special responsibility in Canada of providing these additional jobs.
April 20, 1977

Perhaps the greatest difficulty facing the minister and the country is the problem of increasing our productivity. This is the greatest challenge to business, labour and government. We have developed a very high standard of living over the past few decades, mainly through trade. Even though our industry was less efficient and on a smaller scale than that of other countries, we were able to be competitive. Most of this was due to the fact that wages tended to be low in this country. Now they are equal to most other countries, and in some cases higher than, say, in the United States. The country still has to depend on foreign trade, however, for over 25 per cent of the gross national product, so we must regain the competitive position we lost in many industries over the last couple of years due to spiralling inflation and the resulting increase in the price of products we sell abroad.
This budget seeks to regain our competitive position by controlling inflation and by providing an investment tax credit for the modernization of plant and equipment. More important, it provides an increase in the investment tax credit for research and development programs. Surely, in a time of rapid technological change, a company that is not doing adequate research and development and is not providing innovative programs in the design of products will not be able to maintain a good position in the marketplace. I think this investment tax credit for research and development activity in industry is very important.
The discussions of the last little while which have involved industry, labour and government are equally important for the regaining of our productivity and our share of world markets. Surely, unless those three bodies can agree on a suitable structure for sharing our economic pie, we will not be able to regain our productivity. Therefore, discussions involving government, labour and industry are terribly important if we are to maintain our productivity and sales abroad.
The budget proposals regarding regional development are most significant. The tax investment credit has been extended for three years and for the first time, so far as I am aware, a new fiscal tool has been forged for dealing with regional development. The new investment tax credit for areas like northern Ontario will rise to I'h per cent. In the areas not designated under DREE it is 5 per cent. In the maritimes the credit will increase to 10 per cent. I suggest to the minister that he ought to consider raising the credit in all DREE areas to 10 per cent. At present I think he will find that economic forces which attract industry to southern Ontario rather than the north, especially to the big cities, are very strong. So strong are those forces that an investment tax credit of at least 10 per cent will be necessary as an incentive to attract new industry to many slow-growth areas of Canada.
I note that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) said in this debate that $580 million had been spent under the Regional Development Incentives Act, and that that sum had created some 127,500 new jobs in DREE areas since the beginning of the program. I point out that the
The Budget-Mr. Foster
investment tax credit has been extended as well to research and development projects. This will have an important bearing, as well, on DREE areas. By making available such an investment tax credit the government is clearly signalling to business and industry that it wants them to establish their operations in designated areas. If they do as the government wishes, they will be eligible for a grants, and their taxes will be reduced as well.
In the past few years many people have criticized the DREE program. Some say it has not been overly successful, that businesses have gone broke and that the government is fighting the natural economic forces in the country. I think, if one looks carefully at the origin of such criticism, one will find that it comes mostly from areas not designated and, therefore, not receiving the benefits of the DREE program. Let us keep that fact in perspective. As the minister said, the program has created 127,500 new jobs in the slow-growth areas of the country. Surely that is an adequate indication of its value.
The DREE program perhaps is most important for the small businessman or the small entrepreneur who does not have a great deal of technical ability or know-how with which to expand or develop a new industry. This program shows such entrepreneurs that the government wants them to establish their operations in slow-growth areas of the country and will give them part of the money with which to do it. Now there is the investment tax credit as well to give encouragement to local entrepreneurs.
Last week I had the privilege of attending the opening ceremonies of a cabinet-making concern in Sault Ste. Marie- Fiore Cabinets Limited. Let me tell hon. members the circumstances of the case because I think it is typical of DREE projects. The head of this company had emigrated to Canada in the 1960s, gone to work in the steel plant and had begun a small, part-time construction business of his own. He began making cabinets, cupboards, staircases and other high quality cabinet materials. In the past few months he put together a small plant with a capital investment of a little over $100,000. The plant will employ between eight and ten people. He is making a high quality product which will be consumed in his immediate area. He said to me that the business is like a dream come true. The amount of the DREE grant in this case was some $18,000. Surely that is a small amount of money to pay for helping to establish a successful plant which will employ from eight to ten people. That is not much money to spend for the creation of such new employment.
It seems to me that a new enterprise begins as an idea. In addition, the entrepreneur must have skill, or business knowhow, and capital. If you put all these factors together, you produce a successful business venture. But the most critical factor is business know-how. Skill in business, or ability to carry out one's business aims, is most important and hard to find. The DREE program attempts to help the small entrepreneur realize his aims. Often lack of capital is a problem. The DREE program can help a small entrepreneur in this regard.
4830

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Foster
It is interesting to note that in Sault Ste. Marie some $85 million worth of capital investment has been stimulated by the DREE program. To date, that program has assisted 19 projects and has been instrumental in creating 1,347 new jobs. All this has been done, I believe, with the expenditure of some $13 million under the DREE program in that one city.
I suggest that in order to aid development, including the regional development program, it would be useful to establish in northeastern Ontario a DREE office to serve that area. At present people in northeastern Ontario must travel either to Thunder Bay or to Toronto to seek assistance or advice. A few weeks ago I met in Toronto with officials of DREE, the Ontario Development Corporation and an entrepreneur who wanted to start a new plant in the Algoma riding. Since the regional office is located in that city, we were able to sit down to discuss the project with officials. We discussed its virtues and how it could be organized.
Unfortunately, that kind of facility, that kind of convenience is not available in northeastern Ontario. The office is located in the principal city of Ontario, where the program does not actually operate. People who must drive, say, 500 miles or 700 miles to the district office in Thunder Bay, or the regional office in Toronto, may be discouraged from making inquiries to determine if their projects are viable or if they can qualify for a grant. For this reason I was pleased to note that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion yesterday, in reply to my question, indicated that he hoped to announce some time in the next few weeks a new office to serve northeastern Ontario.
We can do other things to stimulate economic activity in slow growth areas of Canada like northern Ontario. For instance, we could decentralize the operations of industry, especially of Crown corporations and government departments. Let me be specific. The people of the north shore area of Algoma district are interested in seeing the new uranium refinery for Ontario established in their area. The refinery would create between 150 and 200 new, permanent jobs and between 300 and 400 jobs during the construction phase. We have the uranium mines operating at Elliot Lake. They produce some 5,000 tons of yellow cake a year at present. This production in the next seven or eight years will be expanded to around 9,000 tons of yellow cake a year. That is truly a massive increase in production. It will result in an expansion of that community from around 10,000 or 11,000 people today to around 30,000 by the year 1985, and perhaps even more.
There is very great public support in the north shore area for a uranium refinery to be located there. Practically every municipality has supported this proposal by resolution. Chambers of Commerce have supported it, and other citizen groups. If it makes sense for us to provide grants to industry to locate in slow growth areas, surely it makes good sense for Crown corporations to locate their facilities in the slow growth areas of northern Ontario.

This area of the north shore has gone through great economic ups and down during the past ten years, with the uranium boom and bust of 1959 and the lumbering boom and bust of 1969. It has left much of the area deprived of any real economic activity during the past eight to ten years. A new industry of this magnitude would provide an important industrial tax base for the area, new job security and a whole new economic outlook for the future as it relates to secondary manufacturing and processing industries.
Another area of decentralization I would like to see take place by the federal government relates to the Department of Transport. There have been recent indications by the Seaway authority that they want to cut back their activity at the Sault ship canal. That is a very backward move. They should be looking to expansion of that lock and development of additional transportation facilities, not cutting back at a time when that important canal should be expanding the transportation of goods during the coming years. The Sault Ste. Marie-St. Mary's River locks handle 90 million tons of cargo a year. The Montreal to Lake Ontario area handles only 48 million tons. The Welland lock system handles 59.9 million tons of cargo per year. This gives some indication of the importance of the Sault lock.
We have received some encouragement from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). He has ordered a review of the feasibility of establishing a new and larger lock for Sault Ste. Marie. At the same time, he has reversed the decision of the Seaway authority to cut back the night shift and ordered that it continue until the results of the study are known. We are going to see a very great expansion in shipping in this area over the next 25 years. At the same time, the Department of Transport should be looking into the feasibility of establishing a new coastguard base at Sault Ste. Marie. In any event, new facilities will be required on the upper Great Lakes. A new coastguard base would not only provide employment but ensure better control of shipping, ice breaking and pollution control.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is to be complimented for accurately assessing the difficult dilemma facing Canada today; that is, the need to stimulate our economy while at the same time avoiding a further increase in inflation and an increase in the federal cash deficit. Unfortunately, the announced restraints in federal spending will be more than offset by the inflationary forces at large in Canada today. Our present government has been the author of a tax burden upon Canadian families which has risen from 12.9 per cent to 18.6 per cent of total income. The government has now told
April 20, 1977

Canadians that they are living too extravagantly, while presenting a budget that carries a $7 billion deficit.
Government is more than a symbol to Canadians, more than a focus for their hopes and aspirations. It is the model; it is the pace-setter. In that role it is critical that those who lead our country provide the kind of image which encourages Canadians to believe that the restraint which they practice in their own homes is part of a larger effort to run a tight ship or a lean ship in Ottawa. Such restraint is critical in a budgetary sense as a part of a fight against the two-headed monster, unemployment and inflation, that is eating away at our quality of life. The government of Canada, in its administration and in its management of programs, must set an example. I truly believe that as Canadians we should not only be troubled but ashamed of that deficit. If it were wartime, yes-but not in this day and age. I am a baker, not an economist, but that troubles me. My grandfather had a saying that people who are not afraid to roll up their sleeves seldom lose their shirt. Government, industry and every Canadian must roll up their sleeves, but let the government provide the leadership.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The present anti-inflation strategy has been notably unsuccessful. It has been assumed that today's inflation is caused by the same factors which brought about inflation in the nineteenth century. The response of the present government has been to deal with the problem through measures which would have worked against nineteenth century inflation. Despite the use of such anti-inflation tools as tight monetary restraint, as evidenced by the highest interest rates in Canadian history, and the acceptance of severe unemployment, we still have rapid inflation. Also, since 1971 the total take of our GNP by governments in Canada has risen from 38 per cent to 43 per cent, and of that total 80 per cent is at the federal government level.
I believe that there is a myth alive and well in the political planning area of each ministry that an effective government is a spending government. I believe, from talking to public servants who have spoken to me on the doorsteps in the past few months, that they do not believe that. They, like the rest of Canadians, want to see something more innovative in the management of our government services. Perhaps the new word should become "trade-offs". The trade-offs should become a way of life, with no new government program put in force until one comes off the bottom, perhaps an obsolete one, or that we find fat within the system.
There is duplication in business life as there is in government. It is time to take a definite look at that. People have said to me that no local member of parliament should talk in this way. I disagree. I would be an irresponsible citizen if I did not talk now about this kind of trade-off in our government service. Measures to promote restraint in government must go beyond a simple reduction in the number of paper clips used. Government must take a leading role in looking at the fat within its own system. How can the government appeal to labour and management to practice restraint when they them-
The Budget-Mrs. Pigott
selves are the chief culprits in setting an unhealthy pace in waste and ill-planned spending?
Canadians are demanding an accountability from their government. Frankness and action are necessary to restore our self-respect. Such a goal will not be achieved by clever political moves, arrogance and excuses. We need a leadership which will restore a common purpose of self-restraint in the national interest. A program of restraint, hard work, and balanced budgets may be a bitter cure for economic ills, but the lack of such treatment will lead to even more unhappy times for Canada. Taxpayers today expect that if they tighten the belt there must be self-control in Ottawa as well.
Ottawa is still spending at a rate faster than the economy is growing. It has been pointed out that the Anti-Inflation Board has no mandate to ensure that governments take steps to reduce the size of their deficits. Professor Thomas J. Cour-chene, of the University of Western Ontario, in a special study for the C. D. Howe Research Institute suggested that there is simply no viable alternative to Ottawa's setting its own house in order and keeping it that way.
It is easy to talk of restraint. But the Chinese have a saying that "talk does not cook rice". It has been suggested that we still run government on the basis of a philosophy which presumes that the tasks facing Canada are unchanging, whereas it ought to be assumed that, like any other human activities, the functions of government can become obsolete and unproductive sometimes within a short time. We have been content to measure government programs, not by results and performance but by size. Big is beautiful in Ottawa! It follows that a lack of results is taken to indicate not an inappropriate program but the need for increased size. In Canada today, however, the problems which governments face belong to an area of economics in which results are the measurement of an activity.
There is a need to improve government performance. But this involves more than a reshuffling of the organization chart. Government agencies ought to be given specific goals, with a clear timetable and a clear assignment of accountability. This means that a budget should not only outline money to be spent but also that social changes should be expected from the programs. Each year, systematic reports should determine how well targets have been achieved. Every program should be assessed by an audit committee. Castles in the air cost a great deal to keep up.
Then, again, the objectives of each program should be approached through the establishment of clear priorities. When making an assessment of programs, departments which do not spend all their budgets should be given praise. Much more research is needed into ways of managing government programs more effectively. Greater effectiveness in government will be reached through the organized abandonments of programs which are obsolete. One thinks of the famous story told by Mr. Drucker, the management consultant, about the British navy. In 1945 it succeeded in eliminating a position
80012 -27Vi

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Demers
which had been established in 1812-that of a man standing on the white cliffs of Dover with the duty of looking for Napoleon. How many people do we still have in the public service today who are "watching for Napoleon"?
Canadians are demanding, with great justification, a better performance from government. Our post-war affluence must give way to the return to the virtue of thrift and some old-fashioned common sense. Political rhetoric can no longer disguise the fact that ours is one of the world's costliest governmental superstructures.
We must abandon non-productive programs. Tax reforms to restore initiative must be implemented. "Sunset laws" to ensure that the usefulness of government bureaux and Crown corporations is reviewed on a regular basis must be introduced. It is human nature to look for scapegoats, but creating a hostile climate between government, labour and management to point fingers at each other, when we have such great national problems to face as unemployment, inflation and strains upon national unity, is a tragedy.
Today I believe the taxpayers expect from government and from hon. members on both sides of the House a new look at government spending. I urge the Minister of Finance and the government of which he is a part to consider very seriously the plight of Canadians today and to institute real, not imaginary, restraint to the benefit of the economy and of the people generally.
