subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to speak today on as important a subject as the Canadian budget.
I should like to call to the attention of the House certain weaknesses that exist in our present tax system. Though they exist, specially with regard to taxes, I shall address myself mainly to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) because the authority to change or amend income tax legislation lies with his department.
The Liberal party is recognized as being the one that attempts by every means to eliminate regional disparities and in addition tries to do justice to all citizens, young and not so young, and that from sea to sea. As a member for five years now, I have noticed in this regard that in caucus discussions center mainly on changing the laws to adapt them to the needs of the people while applying fairly and equitably to everyone.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the minister some of those failings which, from my point of view, create injustices for Canadians. In my first example, I shall compare the income tax paid by two families made up of the father, the mother and two children. In the first case, the father earns an annual salary of $20,000; in the second, the father earns $10,000, the mother, $10,000 as well, which means a total family income of $20,000 in both cases. When one spouse alone is breadwinner of the family, when he fills out his income tax returns, federal and provincial in the case of the province of Quebec and a few other provinces, he must pay, after statutory deductions, $4,926 in taxes.

When both spouses fill their income tax returns, $10,000 for the husband and $ 10,000 for the wife, the total income tax for both is only $3,728. So the spouse who is the only one filing an income tax return on the family income must pay $1,198 more than if he were completing two returns. Then, when the husband is the only earner in the family, his income tax is 32 per cent higher than if both spouses were completing an income tax return.
I would like to give another example still more glaring. In this case, the family income earned by both spouses is $20,000 in wages, plus $2,000 in interest or dividends. They have two children and, besides the statutory exemptions, they make maximum contributions to a pension plan-20 per cent of the salary-and they are also entitled to the maximum deductions for child care and I suppose they have the maximum deduction for the home ownership savings plan and obviously the deduction for interest.
When the husband is the only one to earn this salary of $20,000 plus $2,000 in interest, only $1,000 in interest is not taxable. He is being denied child care, and home ownership savings are limited to $1,000. When figuring out his income tax, this individual whose family earns a total of $22,000 a year has to pay $3,614 in tax to the province of Quebec and to Canada. On the other hand, his neighbours whose family income is exactly the same, that is $22,000 a year distributed half and half between husband and wife-both entitled to the same deductions as in the first case where only the husband works outside-have $2,000 in non taxable interest income. Child care expenses amount to $2,000, home ownership savings to $2,000 and non taxable interest income to $2,000.
Thus, if you figure out the income tax of both husband and wife, the total amount payable by those two individuals is only $1,087. Therefore, the income tax paid in that case is $2,527 which is less than in the case where only the husband files an income tax return. The result of these disparities leads me to the following calculation. When the whole family income is under the husband's name, his taxes are, would you believe it,' 332 per cent higher than when both spouses send individual income tax returns, this for the same family income.
Yes, 332 per cent higher. Why such a difference? As we all know, the first reason is the progressive increase in tax rates. Thus, when only the husband declares a $20,000 income, the tax rate on the eleventh thousand or on the twentieth is much higher than on the first $10,000 income individually declared by each spouse. Furthermore, if the husband declares $2,000 in interest, he is allowed an exemption only of $1,000, whereas this exemption is $2,000 when both spouses declare this income. Something else, if both are working the child care deduction is $2,000 for two children, but they are denied this deduction when only one of them is working. We face the same problem with the home ownership saving plan. If the husband is the only one working, it is limited to $1,000, but if both are working they are allowed a $2,000 deduction.
April 20, 1977

In addition, if we analyze the statutory deductions, we realize that the basic deduction for the taxpayer who files his federal income tax return for 1975 is $2,090. If his wife does not work, he is entitled to claim only $1,830. This means a loss of $260. As for medical expenses and charitable donations, a personal $100 deduction is granted without receipt, thus couples who file their income tax return can claim that $100 twice. At number 5 of the income tax return, a 3 per cent deduction on wages is granted. Once again, the taxpayer who is the sole breadwinner is restricted to the maximum deduction of $150. If both earn they can claim $300. This is not all, because for your information it is worse at the provincial level since that deduction amounts to $500 per income tax return. Thus a couple filing two returns is entitled to $1,000, but if there is only one breadwinner the exemption is only $500.
Mr. Speaker, I realize on the basis of those examples that our taxation system is grossly unfair to couples when one spouse only is working. Yet, it would be only logical to encourage mothers to stay at home as much as possible to raise their children, which would also avoid marriage break ups. As we know, the family is the single most important component in our society. For that reason, I believe that such a situation creates very serious inequalities which the Liberal Party should correct as soon as possible. I hope that before bringing in those measures, we will not wait until a group of non-working mothers starts a lobby.
Far be it for me to dictate how the situation should be corrected, but I might suggest for instance that we should tax the family income instead of the individual's income, as is being done in the United States. I realize that such a procedure would cause other problems. However, the department could consider another way of doing it, by granting perhaps the same deductions to a couple that fills in one return as to those who submit two.
I should be delighted if I finally convinced the hon. members of the House when I acquainted them this afternoon with these serious inequalities, and I hope that the necessary amendments to our tax system will not be long in coming. There is another point which I should like to bring to the attention of the House, Mr. Speaker. I have computed the taxes which a Quebec resident must pay and I have compared them with those which an Ontario resident must pay. For a $20,000 income from employment and with statutory exemptions only, the married person whose spouse does not work and who works in the province of Quebec must pay $5,249 in federal and provincial income taxes, annuities and health insurance, while his Ontario counterpart pays only $4,273. There is therefore a difference of $976 or 23 per cent between the Quebec resident and the Ontario resident.
That gap will grow wider in 1976 because the Quebec government did not gear personal income tax to the cost of living, as was so often promised. Therefore the fact that personal income tax in Quebec is much higher than that of their neighbours in Ontario has several effects. For instance, I know some employees of the House of Commons and from private industries in Ottawa who would rather rent an apart-
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
ment in Ontario instead of Quebec precisely because of that income tax differential. That tax gap results in a substantial emigration from Quebec to Ontario.
Again we Quebecers often wonder how come so many companies take their head offices out of Quebec into other provinces. Several factors naturally are involved. However one aspect favours such an emigration. These company administrators who make their decision about the site of their head offices are human indeed and when a decision has to be taken, they do keep in mind the lesser taxes they will pay if they settle outside Quebec, and that greatly influences their choice. And my earlier calculation revealed that provincial tax on a $20,000 income is $976 more in Quebec than in Ontario.
Many corporate directors however have incomes high above the $20,000 mark, and then the extra tax they must pay in Quebec increases in proportion. It is therefore my view that the province of Quebec should review their tax system to make it more similar to the Ontario one.
There is also another point I would like to make. Recently, when I visited a sports goods shop in Montreal, I saw a baseball glove made in Hong Kong and imported by Jelinek Imports Limited. There was also a baseball mitt made in Taiwan and imported by the same company. There was even a Canadiana tennis racket, unfortunately the Canadiana brand was quite misleading because it was made in Taiwan. There were also tennis balls from England, all imported by Jelinek Imports Limited. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, we have here a member for High Park-Humber Valley called Otto Jelinek, who opposed very vigourously the decision by the minister to reduce Canadian import quotas to support our Canadian manufacturers. It is my hope that the same member is no longer a shareholder of Jelinek Imports Limited.
I would like to conclude on these remarks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one speaks in a budget debate one can talk about many of the very serious economic problems we are facing in this country, or one can speak about the high rate of unemployment we have in Canada.

We could not refer to the issue of national unity and that of the province of Quebec remaining within Confederation, but this afternoon, rather, I would like to speak on the question of a national food policy and a national policy for Canadian farmers.

I am very tempted to speak about the province of Quebec, a province that I love. I am tempted to speak about why I think we should all stay together and why we have to recognize many of the legitimate aspirations of the people of Quebec.
Since I only have a few minutes, I want to spend it talking about policies for food and agriculture. There are many rumours going around the country that the cabinet is going to

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
make a decision on national food policy very shortly. I am very fortunate to have here in the House the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott). I want to say a few words about what that food policy should be and some of the fears I have.
I have a fear that there is going to be a bias in that food policy away from farmers, away from the family farm and away from the orderly system of marketing that we have known in this country for so many years. Farmers have fought for that system in the past in order to build it up. Many things have happened recently that lead me to that conclusion. I sincerely hope I am wrong.
We had the Food Prices Review Board and many of the statements that it issued from time to time. It had, in my opinion, a definite anti-orderly marketing or anti-marketing board approach. Then we had the very famous DM-10 report which took a very similar position. It took a position against the orderly marketing approach, the farmers' organizations and the marketing board approach. A copy of the paper that came out of the meeting that the minister talked about today in the House very recently leaked to the press. It was a meeting that many people were invited to, according to him.
Some people from the marketing boards went to that meeting. One of the biases in that report, confirmed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House today, is that it takes a negative point of view vis-a-vis some of the marketing boards and orderly marketing in this country. I say to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that the time has come in this country to look at food policies and pricing and not just at marketing boards. Not all marketing boards are perfect. I am not going to be the person who says that they are. We must not just look at marketing boards; we must look at all the other factors that go into the pricing of food in Canada. We have the retailers, the processors, the wholesalers, the transporters and the advertisers.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs applauding. I will put his applause on the record. I am glad to see that he is very much in favour of that approach, so that when we do have a future food policy those things will be taken into consideration.
There are many things that concern me. First, there are myths. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in Winnipeg of myths very recently. There is one myth that we have to knock down, and that is that farmers in the west are very wealthy. We had high grain prices for a while, but grain prices have now started to drop. The price of grain has dropped drastically over the last year.
Farm income in Canada, on a gross basis, dropped from January, 1975, some 31 per cent according to Statistics Canada. Gross farm income in the west dropped by some 38 per cent over the same period of time. The prairies are a major factor there. There are a lot of people in western Canada and, indeed, right across the country who are concerned about the future of agriculture and about the security of farm income.

That question must be a very large part of any future food and agricultural policies in Canada.
Over the years we have built up many marketing boards and various stabilization plans, federally and provincially, that are a very important part of the food and agricultural policies of this country. I would like to deal with this area in three sectors this afternoon. First, I am concerned about the availability of food in this country. All of us know that there is the potential of a grave food crisis in the world. The world's population is about four billion. That may double to about eight billion people by the year 2000.
Fifteen thousand to 16,000 people are dying every day of starvation. Over half the population of the world is undernourished. If we cannot feed them now, what are we going to do with them in the future when more and more farmland has been plowed under? Quality soil in Canada is becoming less, as it is in many parts of the world. I think Canada has an obligation to the world food scene. Its obligation is not just in terms of aid; it is in terms of offering to the people of the developing countries technical assistance and expertise to make sure that they become self-reliant and can produce their own food.
I am convinced that most countries in the world can produce enough food to feed themselves. We can offer them the assistance which they so badly need. Many people think we are already doing that; that we are already helping to develop these countries. It came as quite a shock to me to Find out a few weeks ago that the developed world imports more protein from the developing world than we export to them. There is a net shift in a negative direction; we are going in the wrong direction.
A lot of the very high quality land in Third World countries is used to produce luxury crops for export. They produce tobacco, bananas, coconuts and all kinds of luxury foods for the western world. They use their best land for that and they try to feed their people on food grown on secondary land. As a result, there is famine in many countries which should be able to support themselves. This situation has increased since a few years prior to the so-called green revolution.
The second problem we have concerning the availability of food is feeding ourselves. Many Canadians say we could easily feed ourselves. The Department of Agriculture says that 250 acres of land is going out of production every day in Canada. That is about ten acres an hour of good farmland. Only 4 per cent of our country can be farmed. Most of our country is rock, timber and water. If we keep taking the best farmland in Canada out of production, such as in the lower mainland of British Columbia, the Montreal area and the southern Ontario area, we may not be able to feed ourselves a few years down the road.
The Science Council of Canada has said that by around the year 2000 we in this country might become a net importer of food. How do we reverse that once we have paved over a lot of our best farmland? If we had a sensible policy, we would stop building schools, factories and hydro lines across much of our better farmland. If we had a sensible land use policy in this
April 20, 1977

country, much of which is under provincial jurisdiction, we could have federal leadership regarding land banks and zoning. We could build cities, factories and suburbs on land of much poorer quality. That could be done if we took land out of the private sector and made it a social responsibility. We should preserve good land for growing food. That could easily be done in Canada.
The other matter I am concerned about when it comes to the availability of food is self-sufficiency in food. There are many crops in this country which we could and should be producing if we wanted to feed ourselves. Many people say it does not make economic sense, that we should import many foods from tropical countries, from California and Florida; but may I remind you that many of those places will have problems with growing food in the future and may not have a food surplus to export to us. Many of those places may have a shortage. If we are going to get it in the first place, we will have to pay a high price for it, and that is not good for our consumers.
The other things that will work to our disadvantage if we are not self-sufficient in many of the commodities we can produce is that we will lose farmers who could be farming; we will lose food processors, packagers and the secondary industry that could be processing, packaging and distributing Canadian food; we will lose jobs, money and productivity; and we will suffer a balance of payments problem. Those are a few of the problems we will have because of the fact that we are not self-sufficient in many of the basic foods. There are various commodities one could mention which we import from the United States and process in southern Ontario, in the middle of some of the best farmland in north America, when we could be processing Canadian foods. Ontario peaches are a good example of that.
The second problem we have when it comes to food policy is the manner in which we produce food. How do we produce it? Do we produce it through the tried and successful methods of the family farm? Many people laugh at that and say it is nostalgic and sentimental. A number of studies have been made which show that the most efficient way of producing food is on the family farm. The whole farming family is part of the unit. They are proud of that unit and they produce efficiently. Their productivity has gone up faster in the last 20 or 30 years than that of any other segment of the economy. We must not forget that that is the most efficient way of producing food. I would not want to see food produced in this country by huge corporations that are integrated right down to the farmstead, taking over all the farmland. That will happen if we do not protect some of the institutions that the farmer wants for himself.
We need orderly marketing in Canada. There has been criticism of marketing boards. The paper referred to by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs a few days ago was critical of them. It referred to the number of egg producers who went out of business between 1965 and 1975. We did not get CEMA, the national egg marketing board, until
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
1975, and I hazard a guess that if we did not have orderly marketing of eggs in provinces such as Saskatchewan and Manitoba we would soon be down to one or two large producers. At least we have been able to save some smaller units because of national marketing boards. If you have these products out on the open market without any supply management, you will shortly have just a few companies which will capture the whole market and there will be a monopoly of corporations.
A marketing board is nothing more than an organization to plan production, just like trade unions or business associations, so that the private sector can get together and plan production. You would not think of General Motors producing eight million more cars than they can sell. You would not think of any corporation producing many more products than it could sell. I do not see why farmers should be called upon to produce more products than they can sell. That is why they need marketing boards, and that is why they need orderly marketing. That is why they have to plan their production like everyone else in this country.
If you do not have that, you will have huge corporations such as Kraft and McCain's in the maritimes, and a few other companies, producing food in Canada. Then what will the consumer be paying? What will the housewife in Sudbury be paying for meat, fruits and vegetables? That is the fear I have. There is a bias, particularly in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, against marketing boards. Some people may say that marketing boards may do more for big producers than for the small ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps in some cases marketing boards are better for big farmers than for small farmers. But we can reform marketing boards.
We should look at the whole question of the capitalization of quotas. I do not see why quotas cost so much when farmers want to start producing a commodity. Basically, quotas should not cost money. They should be allocated, first of all, to the small guy who wants to start out, or the smaller farmer so he can have an efficient unit. Quotas should not be allocated on a percentage basis to all farmers involved in producing a certain commodity, because the big farmer gets bigger, and although the small farmer also gets bigger, he does so at a much slower pace than the big farmer. In that way you help the big guy more than you help the small guy. But if you did not have a marketing board, the small guy would not be there at all, and even some of the bigger guys would not be there. They would all be gobbled up by the huge corporations.
So let us keep the marketing boards. Let us allow them a bit of a bias for the small producer, and let us have government policy with a bias for the young people involved in farming. Let us give them opportunies and breaks and get them into the marketplace. That is the bias we need in a national food policy. Then not only do you have security of supply and security of income for farmers, which is gradually going up, but you will also have a stable price for the consumer. We

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
would not have the constant fluctuation of price that we have in so many commodities in Canada.
The other thing I am concerned about when it comes to how we market food is that there is also a tendency of going toward an open futures market by some members of the cabinet. I am thinking of the Minister of Transport in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang). I think that is a dangerous trend. There is Cargill Grain which is now competing with the wheat pools owned by the farmers in the prairies. It is a huge company which operates 40 or 50 companies around the world. Its sales a couple of years ago amounted to $9 billion. It is so big and strong that it makes a wheat pool look like a mouse compared to an elephant. I do not want to see that type of development continue, because if it does it will drive away grain producers as it did many farmers in Canada.
It is important that we look at the second problem I have raised and make the decision that we will have the farm family as our basic unit of production, that we will have orderly marketing as a system for marketing their products, and that we have a guaranteed income system so that the farmer can have a secure income which goes up with the cost of living in Canada.
In the remaining minutes left to me I want to talk about the third aspect of food production. If we produce food in an orderly marketing way, and if we produce enough of it, is the food going to be good enough? Will the quality of that food be good enough? I suggest that the quality of food in Canada and in the world is going down each year. Recently, in the United States, a report was prepared by Senator McGovern. It stated that in the United States about six out of ten of the major diseases which cause death have possible links to bad diet. The World Health Organization recently stated that up to 90 per cent of cancers might be caused by environmental factors, food being one of them. Of course, there are others such as smoking and pollution.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not smoking.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The member from the tobacco growing country says "Not smoking". Drinking is another factor. Many of these factors could be caused by bad diet. Every person in Canada eats on average over 100 pounds of sugar a year, a commodity which we do not have to consume because our bodies produce enough sugar from carbohydrates. This is what happens in a modern man's diet. There is more processing, more artificial food, more fabricated and phony foods, like wood bread which we discovered in the United States, are coming on the market each and every day-junk food, heavy calorie foods. There are today more fat people and more unhealthy people than we have ever had. Over 1,800 chemicals are put into our food supply on a routine basis, and probably another 1,000 chemicals are used from time to time. Most of those chemicals are not present for any positive, nutritious reason. Granted, some are, but most are not. Some are present to make bread white, to make chickens yellow, to produce more volume or to absorb water.

Cellulose is present in ice cream. Cellulose is actually wood pulp which makes ice cream more crispy. Most additives are put into foods to make them more profitable and convenient for food companies. They are supposed to be more attractive to the consumer. I do not know why we have to do these things. Packaging and advertising contain the same bias. We are teaching people to eat crappy food, junk food. When I sit with my three-year old watching television and watch the child respond to advertisements about high sugar food, about McDonald's and about french fries, I become angry. People are being socialized at an early age.
In the government's food policy, which I hope is coming very shortly, I hope the quality of food will be of prime importance.
I hope we will have tough legislation in this country so there will be fewer additives and fewer artificial and synthetic foods.
I hope we can produce food for the purpose of nutrition. Recently, the vice-president of a large supermarket company in Canada came to my office and told me that food companies can sell nutritious food as easily as the junk food they are selling today. All they have to do is slap on a label, put a product through the advertising system and that product can be sold very easily. I suggest that what we need is strong government legislation so that we can have good, wholesome and nutritious foods on the market.
Just to summarize very quickly, we need a food system which will assure availability of food for the future, which will reserve our farmland for farming, which will make us self-sufficient in food, which will produce many of the crops and commodities we are not producing today, so that we can process them here and give Canadians jobs and which will provide orderly marketing and good quality food.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to participate in any debate in this House. Although I generally disagree with the philosophy of hon. colleagues to my left, I must indicate without hesitation that I share some of the concerns just expressed with reference to the development of the formulation of a national food policy. I think that people like Colonel Sanders, Ronald McDonald and H. Salt have done more for the food industry in this country than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) put together. One has to admit that this government has been responsible, particularly in recent months, for a long list of records: record inflation, record expenditures, record unemployment levels, record deficits-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Kidnapping.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-record uncertainty, confusion, confrontation, mistrust and division throughout Canada. These are records which are unacceptable to the Canadian people, which will no longer be tolerated and which the government will soon live to regret. As a result of its lack of performance, its lack of adequate and appropriate action and its lack of programs and policies, this government has created a situation in this country
April 20, 1977

whereby the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on budget night found himself almost completely paralysed. The contents of his budget provide ample evidence of this rather pathetic circumstance.
One journalist quite accurately described the task of the Minister of Finance as being similar to one crossing a minefield while wearing snowshoes. Such an observation, although to a large degree true, does not by any means let the minister off the hook. The minister has been a member of this government since 1962. He has been a major policy and decisionmaker since 1970, and consequently he has been a major contributor to the present state of our economy and to the position he found himself in on budget night.
Not desiring to be accused or guilty of being ungrateful for small mercies, I want to grasp this opportunity to welcome the tax cuts to medium and low income earners. At a time when we have over one million unemployed, the incentives to business and the additional $100 million to the $358 million make-work program are absolute necessities. The obvious question that must be posed, of course, is this: Are these suggested measures sufficient to provide the jobs required? In addition, we must know whether this budget will indeed provide greater stimulus to the business and industrial sectors of our economy, and when we can expect the resulting impact to reflect positively on our over-all economic performance.
Most who have commented since the introduction of the budget have expressed real doubt that the proposals are significant enough to provide much hope for any major improvement in terms of additional employment, reducing the inflation rate or strengthening our economic performance. In fact, the Minister of Finance has since admitted the fact that he did not have tools of significant magnitude at hand to be able properly to effect a reduction in the rate of unemployment. Many business leaders have indicated that because of the lack of stable economic conditions, the lack of investment capital and their poor competitive position, they are operating at 20 per cent less than capacity. This being the case, in many instances it is highly unlikely that the extra incentives provided in this budget will be fully utilized. Consequently, little benefit will be reflected in the business and industrial sectors and the number of new jobs created will fall far short of the number required.
I want to make a brief comment at this point on the government's approach to make-work programs. There has been much said and written about these programs, both for and against. Many examples of very worthwhile and excellent projects could be sited yet on the other hand many wasteful, useless and otherwise bad examples can be found. Dissatisfaction has been expressed from time to time from various quarters of the House regarding the distribution and allocation of funds.
Personally, I have no argument with the allocation of funds, nor do I have any argument with projects approved in my constituency. Indeed, by comparison local funding has been adequate and fair. The selection of good projects has been assured by an extremely dedicated, geographically representative, knowledgeable and hard working constituency advisory
The Budget-Mr. Wise
group. I point to their activities with pride and I am grateful for their sincere interest and assistance. I am certain that if other expenditures made by the government were as carefully screened as those by the Elgin constituency group and, indeed, by other committees, our economy would be in far better shape today than it is.
However, having made those observations I am concerned about the guidelines laid down for the Canada Works program. Sponsors are required to submit applications which are for purposes not considered to be part of their ongoing duties or responsibilities. What this really does is place greater temptation and emphasis on the sponsors in many cases to request projects which could be unnecessary, basically nonessential and consequently of less benefit to the community.
I firmly believe that the guidelines governing the old local initiatives program, which allowed municipalities, boards of education, conservation authorities and similar public bodies, to secure funds for their day to day operations and activities, were far more effective and beneficial. These organizations, if I can refer to them using that terminology, should have the necessary structure to deal capably with administrative responsibilities. Second, when such organizations received funding, every taxpayer and resident in the community benefited from the program. Third, these programs were usually labour-intensive. Jobs were thus created for many unskilled workers, and this certainly is a major area of current concern.
I hope the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) will carefully assess the projects in the first phase of the Canada Works program and compare them with those under the local initiatives programs in terms of dollars spent, jobs created, project worthiness and community benefit. I request that if a clear indication is evident that greater value can be achieved by revising the present Canada Works guidelines, the minister take immediate and appropriate action.
I want, now, to deal with an area with which I have some special responsibility in this House, namely, agriculture. This budget is in keeping with the long-standing Liberal tradition of total disregard for the agricultural industry. Like the previous budget, one small concession is given high profile attention, while on the other hand buried deep in the documentation a few more nails are driven into the coffin. Mr. Speaker, this government has chosen to continue its long-standing policy of undermining the agricultural industry. It has given a great fanfare to deferral of capital gains if re-invested in another like enterprise, while at the same time-if you can imagine it-it has further lowered tariffs on canned meats, many vegetables both fresh and processed, and some juices such as tomato juice.
Mr. Speaker, the capital gains deferral provision was long overdue. We welcomed that change because it was one of the many changes that my colleagues and I had been requesting since the harsh and unfair impact of the tax became evident. I know that my colleagues, the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldi-mand (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Halifax-East
4838

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Wise
Hants (Mr. McCleave), have dealt very extensively with this subject on many occasions. This budget fails, once again, to extend capital gains tax deferral to family farm corporations and to moneys received from all forced sales. It fails to provide any recognition for inflation and land appreciation values, much of which results from factors that have no relationship to the production capacity of the land for the calculation of capital gains tax payments.
I suggest that an amendment to deal with this situation is absolutely necessary if the government is to continue the application of capital gains on farmlands and farm properties. I am told that in many cases, because of inflation and the dramatic increase in farmland prices, the deferral of a tax payment has actually resulted in a far greater payment and hardship than if no deferral provision existed at all.
Mr. Speaker, some sweeping changes must be forthcoming in tax policy. They are long overdue. The industry is deserving of them and it is imperative that they come immediately. It would seem to me, since the sale of farmland in itself has long provided the pension and retirement funds of farm operators, that a "once in a lifetime" exemption from capital gains tax would be in order and quite acceptable. Mr. Speaker, given the fact that the application of capital gains has in itself been inflationary and has contributed largely to increased land values, perhaps it would be advisable to consider the removal of their application on farmlands and farm property generally.
Another area of great concern that again has been ignored by the Minister of Finance is the inability of the farm wife to receive income for her contribution to the general operation of the farm enterprise. More often than not, her knowledge and influence and day to day functions are many and varied and certainly are most beneficial in the over-all success of the business. Under present law one is able to hire, pay and deduct as an allowable expense almost anyone except the farm wife. The only way that women or children who work on family farms can be entitled to payment is if the farm is incorporated. If this is done, they pay lower taxes on the first $100,000 and pay their legitimate labour fees on the farm. But there is a catch. If they choose to pass the farm on to the next generation, then they lose the tax deferral provision.
It is a pity the minister has ignored the many briefs and representations that have been made by our most responsible and respected farm organizations. I want to draw attention to a fine brief on the subject of taxation as it relates to agriculture, prepared and presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture-obviously in vain. One of the most progressive recommendations deals with special rules that would enable a farmer to assign land to an appropriate form of retirement savings plan so that he may retain his funds for investment use on the farm.
In general, when a taxpayer invests in a retirement savings plan, he has to save out of his income sufficient money to make that investment. This is very advantageous from an income tax point of view, and most taxpayers are not too severely restricted in the sort of investment they may choose to make. A farmer, however, is typically under constant pressure to make

additional investment in his farm to maintain its technological efficiency and economic viability. This severely limits the ability of the farmer to take advantage of the tax deferral benefits of investment in registered retirement savings plans and also reduces the amount he may make available from his income for investment, because it must be an after-tax amount.
It is proposed that to correct this situation a special provision be made that would permit the farmer to obtain tax deferral by assigning part of the value of his land each year to a registered retirement savings plan account. The existence of the deferred tax obligation involved could be registered as a lien on the land, so that it could not be sold or transferred without automatic notice to the tax authorities. It should be provided that the farmer could at any time, if the funds became available, reduce or dissolve the special RRSP account by investing part or all of the amount in that account in another RRSP. In the event of the death of the farmer the RRSP could be inherited by the spouse; or if inherited by others it would become payable. It would be our expectation that such a provision would be used sparingly by farmers, in fact, but that it would be exceedingly useful to some-especially young farmers with heavy investment requirements.
Mr. Speaker, I want now to direct your attention to three areas of major concern, areas which the government continues to do almost nothing about and no doubt would prefer that we forget entirely. These three areas are farm income, farm input costs, and tariff inequities. Reports from Statistics Canada indicated a decline in farm cash receipts during the year 1976. Basing its findings on preliminary estimates of farming operations in all provinces except Newfoundland, the agency shows a drop to $9,737 billion from $9,877 billion in 1975, a total decrease of $140 million.
At the agricultural outlook conference last December economists told delegates in attendance that net farm income would decline for the second consecutive year in 1977. This year's drop is estimated at more than 20 per cent, to $3.36 billion from $4.25 billion last year. Yet the Minister of Agriculture continues to pat himself on the back and make references to himself as the best agriculture minister that farmers in this country have ever had.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite may applaud, Mr. Speaker, but an examination of the record proves such references to be false, inaccurate, shamefully boastful and untrue. The truth of the matter is that increases in farm input costs far exceed those of farm income, and by an ever-increasing margin. Farm operating costs for 1976 jumped by approximately 11 per cent, and another 5 per cent at least is expected this year. That would be a total increase of 16 per cent over two years. Major factors contributing to these costs are farm machinery, interest on loans, wages for farm labour-if appropriate and satisfactory people can be found-energy costs, and inflated land prices.
April 20, 1977

Fertilizer prices have doubled, generally, since 1972. For example, fertilizers which cost in the neighbourhood of $113 a ton in 1972 today cost about $210. Others which cost $93 and $110 in 1972 today would cost $185 and $225 per ton, respectively. Sprays and chemicals have increased in price by approximately 50 per cent, in some cases even more, during the last five years. For example, materials which for a given quantity would have cost $29 and $70 in 1972 today cost $71 and $93 for the same quantities respectively. Baler twine has doubled in cost. A 100-horsepower tractor which could be purchased in 1972 for $9,800 now costs in the neighbourhood of $20,000. Similarly, a combine priced at $15,000 in 1972 now carries a price tag of over $30,000. Diesel fuel, to give another example, has doubled in price during the last five years and will soon experience another price increase.
The price of most concentrates and livestock rations has tripled. For instance, 16 per cent dairy ration cost $51 a ton; now it costs $160 a ton. The price of poultry ration in the same period has risen from $65 to $174. The price of hog grower has risen from $56 to $160. Beef supplements cost $62 a ton in 1972, but the cost is in the neighbourhood of $140 a ton in 1977.
There is an urgent need, Mr. Speaker, for reform in another area of the Canadian agricultural industry. I am referring to the tariff structure which relates to our agricultural industry and agricultural products. There is nothing in this budget to indicate that this government is prepared to tackle this problem or that it even recognizes that our native producers are suffering unduly because of continuing government inaction. The agricultural industry of this country is burdened with an antiquated tariff structure, many items of which have not been revised for 25 years.
For the horticultural industry in particular the problem is crucial and bears on their continued existence. Briefly, it is simply a matter of unfair competition. For example, Canada has a specific duty on imported fresh and processed vegetables between 1.5 cents and 2 cents per pound. Perhaps this was adequate protection at one time. Unfortunately, by its very nature, this kind of protection is unable to keep pace with inflationary prices. Our competitors, such as the United States and European Economic Community countries, have ad valorem duties in the order of 15 per cent or 20 per cent on the same products. Therefore, as prices go up the tariff goes up and protection is automatic, regardless of price levels. We must not allow our fruit and vegetable producers to suffer the fate which befell the sugar beet producers of southwestern
The Budget-Mr. Tessier
Ontario, in the late 1960s when stiff and unfair competition from foreign producers drove them out of business.
No one in this House should need to be reminded of the damage imports of offshore beef last year did to our beef industry. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) ably raised this point last evening. Oceanic imports increased by about 57 per cent over the level of the previous year as low priced beef poured into our market. Mr. Speaker, we have a valuable asset in our livestock producers. We do not need to subsidize them to any great extent, but we must not take advantage of them in a world surplus situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join the debate on the budget. I know this is not easy, but neither are solutions easy to find or to apply. The results might be two or even three years of frustration, of search for essential answers that seem impossible to find.
I think this debate is important as it is an opportunity for a member to express his views and suggest how the government should find answers to meet the needs of our constituents. This is why I should like to discuss such important subjects as first, a privileged sector of our economy, agriculture; second, I also wish to mention industrial decentralization and like every member in this House I hope that industrial decentralization will not be just a motherhood statement or a verbal contest but effective decentralization, even in rural areas. Especially as concerns inflation and competition problems, my riding is right next to the American border and we know that in our country the problems of inflation, wages and productivity spell unemployment for our workers.
This debate will also offer a golden opportunity to speak about Canadian unity. That subject seems to haunt several members but I think it is high time to consider the issue of Canadian unity in terms of cost and that some members will have to realize that however laudable it may be to invite Quebec to stay in Confederation, the rest of Canada owes us an answer and we in the province of Quebec will have to pay the price of it.
